outputs.L2:
“Do not seek poetry inside poems.” —Donald Revell

Don’t avoid the question by dressing in skirts.  
Don’t evade gunfire with the help of ducks.  
Your literal face should never confront the music.  
And when you headbutt, employ neither head nor butt.  

A house is not the tool for making a home,  
and poems are no place to hunt for poetry.  
Instead, fill your verses with giraffes;  
release skirted circus monkeys into them.  

Clarify that the wooden nest is no home:  
it is merely a hideout for hunting wild ducks.  
Grip the shotgun at its rhythmic rear  
and point it toward your Muse’s Pringles-shaped, quacking face.  

I’m glad we can speak together, face-to-face.  
Poetry ought to provoke more headbutting.  
Mentioning a brand from the eighties comes at a price, but  
it pays tribute to my adolescent self, forever wearing skirts,  
teaching my sister to “Be the Duck”  
with a potato chip serving as a bill.  

Bring me home, Mr. Revell—  
or settle comfortably into my post–Civil War, Reconstruction face:  
gray eyes, rebellious ears, every duck  
lined up along my vanquished mouth.  

Poems used to possess civility.  
Then war ripped away my skirts  
at the very first frill and exposed my butt.
outputs.L3:
The poem playfully challenges literal-minded approaches to poetry. It warns readers not to look for poetry only in conventional poems, familiar expressions, or recognizably “poetic” language. Instead, it suggests that poetry emerges when ordinary words and phrases are disrupted, reimagined, and made strange.

Much of this disruption occurs through absurd wordplay. Familiar idioms involving skirts, ducks, faces, homes, and headbutting are treated as though they were literal descriptions, producing comic and surreal images. By twisting these expressions, the poem reveals how strange figurative language can become when removed from its usual context. The humor therefore serves a serious artistic purpose: it breaks the reader’s habitual ways of understanding language.

The speaker advocates bringing unexpected elements into poetry rather than relying on predictable conventions. Surreal juxtapositions, verbal accidents, and deliberately incongruous images are presented as sources of creative energy. Poetry is not confined to elevated subjects or polished metaphors; it can be found in jokes, distorted clichés, private associations, and abrupt collisions between unrelated ideas.

This approach also allows personal memory to mingle freely with reflections on poetic craft. Recollections of teenage play with the speaker’s sister appear alongside references to popular culture and the process of writing poetry. These different materials are not arranged into a neat hierarchy. Instead, intimate experience, cultural reference, and literary technique all become part of the same imaginative field, showing how poems can be assembled from the varied fragments of a life.

In the ending, the poem’s playful tone takes on a darker significance through imagery associated with the Civil War and Reconstruction. Conflict is presented as something that destroys the surface of civilized behavior, exposing the body—and perhaps the nation—in a state of vulnerability. The historical references broaden the poem’s argument: just as surreal wordplay strips familiar phrases of their conventional meanings, war strips society of its claims to order and civility. Poetry, in this sense, becomes a way of confronting what lies beneath familiar language and public appearances.
outputs.L4:
The poem begins by challenging the dictum against seeking “poetry in poems.” Rather than refuting this claim through direct argument, it subjects the statement to a series of absurd literalizations. The idea that poetry might be found inside poems becomes a physical, almost comic problem: poetry appears as something that can be hidden, exposed, pursued, or prohibited. By treating an abstract critical principle as if it were a concrete instruction, the poem reveals the instability of the distinction on which the dictum depends. If poetry is not to be sought in poems, where else could it be found—and what, in that case, would make a poem a poem?

This challenge unfolds through surreal imagery and restless wordplay. Images collide without settling into a single symbolic system, while puns and verbal echoes allow one idea to generate another through sound as much as through logic. The poem’s apparent digressions are therefore central to its method. Each attempt to clarify or control meaning produces further associations, and each association opens another imaginative path. What might initially seem nonsensical becomes a demonstration of poetic creativity: language refuses to remain confined to the meaning assigned to it.

The poem also displays a conspicuous awareness of its own form. Its attention to rhythm, meter, and verbal patterning makes the poem seem to observe itself in the act of becoming poetry. Formal control is present, but it does not eliminate disorder. Instead, meter and structure provide a framework within which disruptions become more visible and more energetic. The poem can therefore be both crafted and unruly, disciplined and excessive. Its self-consciousness turns poetic technique into part of the argument, showing that even a statement hostile to “poetry” can become poetic once it is placed into rhythm, repetition, and imaginative sequence.

As the poem develops, its comedy becomes entangled with more personal material. Memory enters the verbal game, bringing emotional and autobiographical associations that cannot be reduced to cleverness alone. Gender likewise complicates the poem’s speaking position and imagery. Questions of identity, authority, exposure, and vulnerability emerge from what initially appears to be an abstract debate about literary interpretation. The poem suggests that efforts to define proper poetic meaning are never entirely neutral: they may also regulate who is allowed to speak, what kinds of experience are considered legitimate, and how bodies and identities may appear in language.

The arrival of Civil War imagery intensifies these tensions. Historical conflict becomes another field into which the poem’s linguistic and personal struggles expand. The war evokes division, violence, national memory, and the impossibility of keeping past conflicts safely contained. At the same time, its presence is not solemnly isolated from the poem’s humor or wordplay. Comic absurdity and historical violence remain uncomfortably adjacent. This collision prevents the poem from becoming either a simple joke or a straightforward historical meditation. Instead, it shows how private memory, public history, gender, and literary form can become entangled within a single poetic movement.

The poem’s escalating structure is crucial to its effect. What begins as a playful response to a critical dictum grows increasingly crowded and exposed. Language accumulates meanings faster than they can be organized, while personal and historical references raise the stakes of the original joke. The poem thus performs the very unruliness that attempts at interpretation or prohibition seek to suppress. It does not merely claim that poetic meaning cannot be policed; it enacts that impossibility.

Ultimately, the poem reveals poetry as something produced through efforts to define, limit, or deny it. A rule against finding “poetry in poems” cannot remain outside poetry once the poem absorbs it. The rule becomes an image, a rhythm, a joke, and a source of further associations. Attempts to protect language from poetic excess only create new occasions for metaphor and invention. By turning prohibition into performance, the poem demonstrates that poetry is inherently unstable, self-generating, and exposed to meanings beyond anyone’s control. The policing of poetry does not end poetry; it becomes poetry’s newest material.
outputs.L5:
### Donald Revell and the Power of “You”

Donald Revell is an American poet known for writing that combines spiritual reflection, vivid imagery, and emotional intensity. In his work, ordinary moments often open into larger questions about love, nature, memory, and human existence.

The word **“you”** is especially powerful in poetry because it creates intimacy. It may refer to a loved one, the reader, a divine presence, or even another part of the speaker’s identity. In Donald Revell’s poetic world, such direct address can make a poem feel both deeply personal and universal.

When Donald Revell speaks to “you,” the reader is invited to participate rather than simply observe. The boundaries between poet, subject, and audience become less certain. This openness allows each reader to find a different meaning in the poem and to experience its questions as their own.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous, irreverent sestina inspired by Donald Revell’s line “We must not look for poetry in poems,” using the end-words poems, skirts, ducks, face, butt, and home.
counterfactuals.output:
### **No Poetry Here, Officer**

We must not look for poetry in poems;  
it’s probably outside, shoplifting skirts,  
or squatting by the courthouse, feeding ducks,  
while dawn applies its hangover of a face  
and God, that cosmic plumber, shows his butt  
through the cracked bathroom window of our home.  

I searched beneath the couch cushions at home,  
finding three dead batteries and no poems,  
then blamed the muse, who merely scratched her butt  
and said, “Try laundromats. Try pleated skirts.”  
Her wisdom wore a mustard-smeared face  
and waddled from the room behind two ducks.  

Those feathered critics, the judgmental ducks,  
had read my latest masterpiece at home;  
one quacked, one hissed, one spat into my face.  
“We must not look for poetry in poems,”  
they chorused, hiking up their little skirts,  
then mooning me with one collective butt.  

I’ve seen more truth tattooed upon a butt  
than in the odes applauded by the ducks  
of academe, all starch and tasteful skirts,  
who praise the void, then Uber safely home.  
They pickle every lightning bolt in poems  
and label it: **DO NOT TOUCH—THE HUMAN FACE**.  

So let the sonnet punch me in the face;  
let every villanelle misplace its butt;  
let parking tickets scan themselves as poems,  
while traffic cops transform at dusk to ducks  
and lead our busted metaphors back home,  
past dive bars full of saints in leather skirts.  

The moon, too drunk for trousers, borrows skirts  
and drags its cratered nonsense through my face.  
I follow, since the idiot knows the way home,  
past angels selling fireworks from their butt,  
past prophets losing arguments with ducks,  
past dumpsters overflowing with old poems.  

Lift up your skirts: behold the moon’s bare butt.  
Put on your bravest face and salute the ducks.  
There’s nothing waiting home but lousy poems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal ars poetica that takes idioms literally—such as “duck the bullet,” “face the music,” and “make yourself at home”—while playfully criticizing conventional ideas about poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
### Ars Poetica with Safety Instructions

First, duck the bullet.  
Give it breadcrumbs.  
Let it paddle circles in the silver pond  
beneath your tongue.

Do not call this *metaphor*.  
Metaphor has arrived in a tweed coat  
to measure the pond  
and explain why water is sadness.

Next, face the music.  
It has a face—  
two cymbals for cheeks,  
a treble clef curled like a question  
through its nose.  
Kiss it if you must,  
but ignore the critic behind the curtain  
checking whether the kiss scans.

Now make yourself at home:  
hammer your ribs into rafters,  
hang a lamp from your astonishment,  
invite the wolves to wipe their feet.  
A good poem has too long been told  
to keep a tidy house—  
no muddy verbs,  
no moon unless approved by tradition,  
no grief without a vase.

Let the cat out of the bag.  
The bag will object.  
The cat will become mayor.  
This is called form.

Break a leg  
and plant it in the garden.  
By spring it will bear small shoes  
filled with bees.

Poetry professors may ask  
what the bees symbolize.  
Tell them the bees are busy.  
Tell them symbolism is in the kitchen  
washing its invisible hands.

At last, bite the bullet—  
but only after it has molted,  
married the duck,  
and learned to sing off-key.

Then put your poem to bed.  
Do not tuck it in.  
Leave the window open.

By morning it should be gone,  
having taken the ladder,  
the dictionary,  
and every rule that said  
a poem must mean  
before it can dream.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a comic postmodern poem in strict sestina form. Include giraffes, circus monkeys, a shotgun, the Muse, Reconstruction imagery, and a nostalgic reference to Pringles.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Republic Pops Its Lid**

In footnotes tall as municipal **giraffes**  
the ringmaster deconstructs circus **monkeys**  
while History mislays Chekhov’s **shotgun**  
and asks who authorized the **Muse**  
to sell bright bunting among Reconstruction **ruins**  
that smell, impossibly, like childhood **Pringles**.  

On road trips, prophecy came stacked as **Pringles**;  
we held the empty cans like telescopes for **giraffes**.  
Now Freedmen’s Bureau clerks inventory the **ruins**,  
while carpetbaggers caucus with circus **monkeys**.  
The Fourteenth Amendment subpoenas the **Muse**,  
who enters a shotgun house carrying a **shotgun**.  

“Relax,” says the prop department, “it’s a symbolic **shotgun**—  
as hollow as the nutritional claims on **Pringles**.”  
A freed schoolhouse raises its chalk to the **Muse**;  
outside, ballots browse the treetops with **giraffes**.  
The narrator denies exploiting the **monkeys**,  
then inserts this denial as scaffolding for **ruins**.  

Moonlight fact-checks the courthouse **ruins**;  
a senator filibusters backward into the **shotgun**.  
Three cymbal crashes enfranchise the **monkeys**,  
who vote for sour cream and onion **Pringles**.  
Above them, punctuation migrates like **giraffes**,  
each comma bending its long neck toward the **Muse**.  

“Your metaphor has fleas,” complains the **Muse**,  
while new-laid railroad tracks stitch through the **ruins**.  
The nation poses for tintypes beside **giraffes**;  
Hope wears a false mustache and unloads the **shotgun**.  
We mourn the vanished foil lids of old **Pringles**,  
that silver dawn before branding colonized the **monkeys**.  

At last the circus unionizes the **monkeys**;  
their contract grants one banana and half a **Muse**.  
History reseals itself with the plastic lid from **Pringles**,  
though footnotes keep escaping into the **ruins**.  
A critic calls the ending “problematic”—then fires the **shotgun**.  
The blanks release confetti shaped like **giraffes**.  

O **monkeys**, rebuild the big top above these **ruins**;  
O **Muse**, autograph the harmless **shotgun**;  
O lost **Pringles**, keep watch from your can with the **giraffes**.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
“We must not look for poetry in poems. —Donald Revell.”

**Outside the Page**

**O**utside, a bus sighs hard against the rain.  
**U**nder my lamp, this sonnet checks its feet.  
**T**he rhyme arrives, a bureaucratic train,  
**S**tamped, numbered, late, and pleased to call it neat.  

**I** joke: the meter keeps the peace in here.  
**D**ownstairs, the landlord raises rent again.  
**E**ach polished line pretends it cannot hear.  
**T**he badge decides whose grammar counts as “men.”  

**H**ere, I confess: my father lost his job.  
**E**ach ballot smiled, then picked his pocket clean.  
**P**ower called hunger an unruly mob  
**A**nd fed our silence to the bright machine.  

**G**ood reader, now the “I” steps off the page.  
**E**nough: a witness must outgrow the cage.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce four stanzas of an edgy contemporary sestina whose recurring line-ending words are “poems,” “skirts,” “ducks,” “face,” “butt,” and “home,” blending absurd wordplay with memories of adolescence and the American Civil War.
counterfactuals.output:
At fifteen I doomscrolled Whitman, then vandalized my margins with poems  
while Sherman marched through homeroom wearing vape-smoke skirts.  
The teacher said history repeats; outside, traffic heckled like ducks.  
I wore acne like a rebel flag stapled badly to my face,  
laughed when Fort Sumter autocorrected itself to Fort Butt,  
and watched each yellow bus surrender us, one by one, to home.  

The dead kept texting “u up?” from Appomattox, asking for home;  
I answered with lowercase grief and catastrophically earnest poems.  
Lincoln loomed from the penny in my pocket, copper butt  
parked on the Memorial, while spring wind court-martialed our skirts.  
At sixteen, every mirror was a firing squad aimed at my face;  
every crush crossed the cafeteria under covering fire from ducks.  

Gettysburg Address? Mine was behind the mall, beside radioactive ducks,  
where we buried a mixtape and swore the future would drive us home.  
Grant photobombed our yearbook; Lee applied a sepia filter to his face.  
We rhymed “emancipation” with “gas-station” in our contraband poems,  
then charged uphill through puberty, bayonets snagged in our skirts,  
history kicking our lockers shut with its enormous iron butt.  

The republic survives, apparently, by shaking its sponsored butt;  
online, Stonewall Jackson sells tactical breadcrumbs to ducks.  
My old classmates have mortgages, pronouns, and weatherproof skirts,  
while ghosts in blue and gray keep missing the last train home.  
I still hear locker doors volley whenever I revise these poems—  
each blank page a nation splitting open along the fault line of my face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
